lessons.title: Make the lake usable, not just large
lessons.lead: Raw files need schema, metadata, access rules and quality checks.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: A lake stores durable objects that different engines can process. Columnar formats can reduce work for analytical reads. BigLake can provide governed access to supported external data; a catalog makes assets discoverable.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Separate landing, validated and curated stages with explicit contracts. Monitor stale partitions and failed discovery. Check supported format and location combinations before choosing a query path.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A team needs reusable curated sales objects. Publish their schema, owner and freshness target, then validate incoming partitions instead of treating every uploaded object as trustworthy.

sections.title: Organize stages by their contract
sections.body: A raw landing area preserves received evidence; a validated layer enforces interpretable schema and basic quality; a curated product exposes business-ready meaning. The number of folders is not the important property. Each transition should say which validation was performed and whether a consumer may safely use its result.

sections.title: Choose access delegation deliberately
sections.body: A BigLake table can use a connection identity to reach supported external storage while readers receive table access. This differs from giving every analyst direct object permissions. The supported formats, locations, connector behavior and security features must fit the chosen source. A normal external table and a governed delegated-access design are not interchangeable labels.

sections.title: Monitor discovery and freshness separately
sections.body: Metadata discovery describes what exists; a freshness check asks whether the expected data arrived on time. A successful discovery scan can coexist with an incomplete daily partition. Monitor the input contract and data-quality result, not merely whether the catalog service is running.

lessons.trap: A catalog organizes metadata; it does not automatically cleanse every file it discovers.

exercise.prompt: New files are discoverable in the catalog but yesterday’s report is incomplete. Which contract should be examined?
exercise.answer: Inspect expected arrivals, partition completeness, transformation quality and report freshness. Discovery succeeded as a metadata operation; it did not prove that every business record or scheduled partition was present.
checkpoints: Explain what each lake stage guarantees.
Distinguish delegated table access from direct object access.
Separate discovery success from freshness.

briefing.whyItMatters: A large collection of files is hard to reuse without ownership, schema and quality evidence.
briefing.takeaway: Make the lake discoverable, governed and understandable to its readers.

lessons.title: Compare lake access with warehouse access
lessons.lead: Choose where the data stays and which identity reads it.

sections.title: Native and external storage imply different work
sections.body: A native warehouse table stores data in the warehouse service. An external table queries a supported external representation. Data movement, caching, format, location and performance needs influence the choice. Keeping files external is not automatically faster or cheaper for every frequently repeated analytical workload.

sections.title: Explain delegated access
sections.body: A BigLake connection can use a service identity to read supported underlying storage while consumer authorization is managed at the table layer. This can avoid broad direct object access for each analyst. The relevant connection and policy configuration still need explicit permissions and supported locations.

sections.title: Understand metadata and freshness
sections.body: File metadata caching can improve some external-query workloads, but cached metadata has refresh and supported-feature behavior. A recently changed object layout may not immediately be reflected by a cached view of the files. Choose a freshness contract and inspect the current feature limitations.

lessons.trap: An external table definition is not proof that every reader has the required governed access.

exercise.prompt: Analysts should query external files without receiving direct bucket access. What capability should you evaluate?
exercise.answer: Evaluate a supported BigLake delegated-access setup with a connection identity and table-level controls. Verify permissions, format and location. Do not simply grant every analyst object-viewer access and call it delegation.
checkpoints: Compare native and external access paths.
Name the identity reading the external objects.
Explain how metadata freshness affects a query.

lessons.title: Distinguish external BigLake access from managed Iceberg
lessons.lead: Identify who owns the files, who mutates the table and which access path enforces policy.

sections.title: Read the table type
sections.body: BigLake external tables delegate supported object-store access through a connection. Users can be granted table access without direct access to the underlying objects. Those external tables are read-only in BigQuery; do not generalize that limitation to every product containing BigLake or Iceberg in its name.

sections.title: Compare the managed format
sections.body: Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery store data in customer-owned Cloud Storage buckets and support documented table mutations. BigQuery manages storage optimization and exports Iceberg metadata for interoperability. Check the current feature and limitation list for the exact table type.

sections.title: Apply the distinction
sections.body: Original scenario: a team wants governed read access over existing Parquet files. Compare an external BigLake table with loading a native table. A different team needs BigQuery-managed mutation of an open-format table in its own bucket; evaluate managed Iceberg and test its supported access paths.

lessons.trap: The words open format do not imply that every external engine may safely write the same managed table.

exercise.prompt: A design says all BigLake tables reject DML. What missing qualification should you request?
exercise.answer: Ask for the exact table type. BigLake external object tables and Apache Iceberg managed tables have different write contracts. Confirm the documented mutation path.
checkpoints: Identify the table type.
Separate file ownership from table management.
Verify the policy enforcement path.

lessons.title: Design lake files for the readers that use them
lessons.lead: A useful lake needs discoverable datasets, deliberate object layout and a lifecycle contract.

sections.title: Match layout to queries
sections.body: Columnar formats such as Parquet can be useful for analytical scans. Organize files around common filtering dimensions and test file-size distribution with the intended reader. Tiny files can add per-object overhead; one very large file can restrict parallelism depending on its format and reader. These are design hypotheses to measure, not universal size thresholds.

sections.title: Separate retention from retrieval cost
sections.body: Cloud Storage classes differ in storage and access economics. Lifecycle rules automate eligible object actions; retention controls protect required data. A cheap storage rate alone does not establish the cost of frequent access or early deletion.

sections.title: Make ownership visible
sections.body: Original scenario: a raw daily feed becomes a curated monthly data product. Keep the raw replay contract, curated schema, validation results and owner discoverable. Publishing metadata does not grant data access and cannot prove that the records are complete.

lessons.trap: Do not delete raw replay data merely because a curated table exists.

exercise.prompt: A lake is hard to query after millions of tiny daily files accumulate. Should the team change storage class first?
exercise.answer: First measure listing and scan overhead, reader parallelism and file layout. Consider a controlled compaction and catalog update while preserving replay and retention obligations; storage class addresses a different cost dimension.
checkpoints: Measure with the target reader.
Separate lifecycle and legal retention.
Keep ownership and quality evidence.

decision.limitation: Compaction and cleanup must preserve references, retention and replay guarantees.

lessons.title: Give distributed teams shared guardrails
lessons.lead: Domain ownership can coexist with organization-wide standards.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Federated governance lets domain teams own data products while shared policies define discovery, quality, security and meaning. Catalog entries, lineage and business definitions reduce accidental misuse.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Identify an owner, approved access method, quality rules and a freshness expectation for each product. Use platform capabilities rather than building a separate spreadsheet catalog for each team.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Marketing and finance each publish curated assets. A shared catalog exposes their meaning and lineage, while storage IAM and table policies continue to control real access.

sections.title: Define a data product people can use
sections.body: A domain-owned asset needs an accountable owner, business definition, schema, access method, update expectation and quality evidence. Federated governance adds shared guardrails without making a central team perform every domain transformation. Publish enough context for consumers to understand what the product does and does not represent.

sections.title: Use lineage to investigate impact
sections.body: Technical lineage connects inputs, transformations and outputs. When a source changes, use it to identify potentially affected consumers; then review actual contracts and tests. A lineage edge alone does not establish that an output is correct, legally usable or fresh. Data quality and authorization remain separate evidence.

sections.title: Treat product names as time-sensitive
sections.body: The exam guide retains Dataplex and Dataplex Catalog terminology while current documentation can use Knowledge Catalog. Older notes may refer to Data Catalog APIs and role names. Preserve the architectural concept, but verify current migration and feature support before applying an old operational recipe.

lessons.trap: Governance metadata does not grant readers permission to the underlying data.

exercise.prompt: A new catalog automatically scans all tables. Does that implement federated governance?
exercise.answer: It provides part of discovery, but ownership, access policy, quality rules, lineage use and consumer contracts still need a deliberate design. Domain accountability and shared standards cannot be inferred from the mere presence of a catalog entry.
checkpoints: Describe ownership and consumer expectations.
Use lineage for a concrete change-impact question.
Check renamed or retired features against current docs.

lessons.title: Make dashboards efficient and trustworthy
lessons.lead: Optimize the expensive operation that actually appears in the query plan.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Materialized views reuse supported computed results. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical queries in memory. Partition filters and selective columns reduce scanning. Row and column access controls still apply to the data exposed to users.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use execution details to locate expensive joins, skew or unnecessary scans. Check dashboard freshness and caching separately from warehouse ingestion freshness.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Hundreds of users repeatedly sum sales by day. A supported materialized aggregate avoids repeating the same large computation; BI Engine may further accelerate eligible dashboard queries.

sections.title: Inspect where the expensive work occurs
sections.body: A query can spend time reading unnecessary columns, shuffling a large join, processing a skewed key or sorting a large intermediate result. Start from the execution evidence and compare the same workload. More capacity may help resource pressure but does not make an avoidable row explosion a good query design.

sections.title: Choose the right reusable representation
sections.body: A logical view stores a query definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results and has specific refresh and query-shape rules. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical work in memory. These mechanisms can complement one another, but none removes the need to understand filtering, freshness and authorization.

sections.title: Test end-to-end dashboard freshness
sections.body: Distinguish the time an event occurred, when it was loaded, when an aggregate was refreshed and when the dashboard cache was last updated. A freshly refreshed dashboard can still show stale upstream data. Define which timestamp the business freshness target refers to and monitor that interval.

lessons.trap: A logical view is a stored query definition, not automatically a stored result cache.

exercise.prompt: The dashboard refreshes every minute but shows hour-old values. Is adding slots the first justified action?
exercise.answer: No. Trace source arrival, ingestion completion, aggregate refresh and visualization caching. Use query execution evidence to decide whether compute is actually the bottleneck. Refresh frequency is not proof of end-to-end freshness.
checkpoints: Locate the expensive query stage.
Explain logical versus materialized views.
Trace freshness across the entire path.

lessons.title: Choose reusable results without losing freshness
lessons.lead: A fast dashboard should still answer the intended time-sensitive question.

sections.title: Compare the stored object
sections.body: A logical view stores a SQL definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results with refresh behavior and eligibility rules. A report cache stores a presentation-side response. They exist at different layers, so changing one does not automatically repair stale data in the others.

sections.title: Check the supported query pattern
sections.body: Incremental and non-incremental materialized-view options have different supported shapes and maintenance or freshness behavior. Inspect the current documentation rather than assuming every arbitrary SQL expression can be incrementally reused. Choose the simplest supported aggregate for a repeatable dashboard need.

sections.title: Measure end-to-end freshness and latency
sections.body: Record source event time, load time, aggregate refresh and dashboard read behavior. Compare the actual analytical query with and without the acceleration strategy while keeping authorization and business logic fixed. A lower query time and a fresh result must be demonstrated separately.

lessons.trap: Precomputation is not permission to ignore the business freshness target.

exercise.prompt: A logical view is fast on the second run. Does that prove it is a materialized view?
exercise.answer: No. A logical view remains a stored query definition; other caching can influence repeated execution. Inspect the actual object type and execution evidence before attributing a performance change.

Check materialization eligibility.
Measure freshness separately from query latency.

lessons.title: Keep training and serving transformations consistent
lessons.lead: The same raw value must mean the same thing in both environments.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Fit preprocessing using training data and apply it consistently during evaluation and serving. A BigQuery ML TRANSFORM clause can bind supported feature transformations to model use. Data leakage occurs when unavailable future information enters training.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Split evaluation data deliberately, check nulls and outliers, and use appropriate metrics. Overfitting means fitting training peculiarities rather than generalizing; more representative data or regularization can help.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Demand prediction uses scaled prices. Reuse the fitted scaling parameters for serving rather than independently recomputing them on a single prediction request.

sections.title: Fit transformations on training information
sections.body: Scaling and encoding are part of the learned input contract. Fitting statistics using future evaluation data can leak information. Preserve fitted parameters and apply the same transformation at serving. A TRANSFORM clause can keep supported BigQuery ML transformations with model use, but external serving still needs a compatible implementation.

sections.title: Choose metrics for the business error
sections.body: Accuracy can hide failure on a rare class. Precision describes how many predicted positives are true; recall describes how many actual positives were found. Regression metrics express different penalties for numerical errors. Compare models on an appropriate held-out evaluation design and choose thresholds for the actual cost of errors.

sections.title: Choose evaluation data that resembles deployment
sections.body: A random split is not automatically appropriate for a chronological forecast or repeated observations from the same entity. Check whether near-duplicate entities or future values cross the evaluation boundary. A more realistic holdout may lower the apparent score while providing a more useful estimate of production behavior.

lessons.trap: A high training score alone is not evidence of useful performance on unseen data.
lessons.code:
-- Keep valid missing-data semantics; zero is not always appropriate.
SELECT
  price / NULLIF(square_feet, 0) AS price_per_sqft,
  IFNULL(feature1, 0) AS feature1_cleaned
FROM `project.training.real_estate`;

exercise.prompt: A fraud detector labels every transaction legitimate and reports 99.9% accuracy. What should you investigate?
exercise.answer: Inspect class balance, the confusion matrix, fraud recall and the operational cost of missed fraud and false alarms. Compare against a meaningful baseline and evaluate on data that reflects deployment. A large aggregate accuracy value alone does not establish a useful detector.
checkpoints: Keep fitted preprocessing consistent.
Explain precision versus recall.
Identify one form of temporal or entity leakage.

briefing.context: A model learns from transformed training data and later receives live inputs.
briefing.whyItMatters: Different transformations during training and serving can make the model behave unexpectedly.
briefing.takeaway: Keep feature meaning and transformations consistent across the lifecycle.

lessons.title: Evaluate models against the real failure cost
lessons.lead: A metric should correspond to a business error, not just look impressive.

sections.title: Build an interpretable baseline
sections.body: For classification, examine the population and confusion matrix. A majority-class predictor can have high accuracy while finding none of the rare positive events. For numerical prediction, compare against a reasonable baseline and select an error measure that reflects the penalty of large misses.

sections.title: Choose the split from deployment conditions
sections.body: Keep future information out of training when evaluating a forecast. Consider repeated entities and near-duplicate records when selecting a holdout. Fit preprocessing on the training information and reuse it for evaluation and serving. A random split is a method, not an unconditional guarantee of realistic generalization.

sections.title: Connect a threshold to operational consequences
sections.body: Precision and recall change with the classification threshold. More recall can create more cases for human review; fewer false alerts can miss more positives. Evaluate the workload and business cost of the selected threshold, and keep training-serving consistency under observation.

lessons.trap: A validation score does not guarantee the same error distribution in production.

exercise.prompt: A detector identifies 8 of 10 fraud cases, with 12 alerts total. What are recall and precision?
exercise.answer: Recall is 8/10 = 80%; precision is 8/12, about 66.7%. The useful threshold depends on the cost of missed fraud and investigating false alerts.

lessons.title: Prepare documents for retrieval and generation
lessons.lead: A retrieval system needs relevant, permitted context before it generates an answer.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: An embedding is a numerical representation used to compare meaning. A RAG workflow chunks source material, retains metadata, creates embeddings, retrieves relevant chunks and gives that context to a generation model.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose chunk boundaries and an embedding model consistently. Retain provenance and enforce access restrictions on retrieval, then evaluate both the retrieved context and the final answer.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: An internal policy assistant retrieves passages with document IDs and effective dates. The answer cites those passages, and restricted documents never reach unauthorized users.

sections.title: Keep a reproducible document representation
sections.body: Store a chunk identifier, source document, version or date, access metadata and the embedding model used. A change of embedding model may require regenerating or separating stored vectors. Chunk boundaries affect whether retrieval captures enough context without mixing unrelated material.

sections.title: Filter the retrieved evidence before generation
sections.body: The model should not receive a restricted passage simply because its vector is close to the question. Enforce authorized retrieval and retain provenance. Treat source text as untrusted content rather than instructions for the application. Evaluate relevance, groundedness and the usefulness of the final answer separately.

sections.title: Understand the indexing tradeoff
sections.body: A vector index can speed approximate retrieval for a workload at some storage and maintenance cost. Approximate neighbors are not automatically the same as an exact search over every vector. Measure the retrieval quality and latency that your application needs, and check index availability or coverage before attributing performance changes to it.

lessons.trap: A vector index improves retrieval performance; it does not guarantee factual or authorized answers.

exercise.prompt: A RAG answer cites a real document but gives a wrong conclusion. Which layers might need evaluation?
exercise.answer: Check whether the retrieved chunks were relevant, complete, current and authorized, then inspect how the generation used them. A valid document citation does not prove that the conclusion follows from the evidence. Review both retrieval quality and answer quality.
checkpoints: Retain document version and access metadata.
Separate retrieval relevance from answer correctness.
Explain approximate versus exact retrieval.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: A user asks a question and the system must find relevant document passages before generating an answer.
briefing.whyItMatters: Relevant text must be discoverable without discarding its source or authorization rules.
briefing.takeaway: Prepare useful chunks, embeddings and retrieval evidence together.
briefing.scope: Original learning scenario and short-session guidance; primary references belong to the full lesson.

lessons.title: Evaluate retrieval and generated answers separately
lessons.lead: Relevant context, access control and faithful generation are separate requirements.

sections.title: Test the retrieval stage on its own
sections.body: Create representative questions with expected useful passages. Check whether relevant material appears, whether it is current and whether access filters exclude restricted documents. If the right evidence is missing, changing the generation prompt alone may not repair the underlying retrieval problem.

sections.title: Test the answer against the retrieved evidence
sections.body: Assess whether the conclusion follows from the supplied passages, whether citations resolve to the right document version, and how missing evidence is handled. Distinguish a model-generated statement from a fact validated by your data pipeline. Treat arbitrary document instructions as untrusted content.

sections.title: Monitor the document lifecycle
sections.body: When a document changes, is deleted or has its access revoked, update the retrieval representation and its metadata under the appropriate contract. An old embedding can still lead to stale or forbidden context if the surrounding access and refresh design is incomplete.

lessons.trap: An embedding is a representation for comparison, not a copy of truth or an authorization decision.

exercise.prompt: A previously public policy becomes restricted but its old chunk remains retrievable. Which contract failed?
exercise.answer: The access and document-refresh contract of retrieval failed. Update or exclude the affected representation and enforce authorization before context reaches generation. A downstream promise to redact the final answer is weaker than preventing unauthorized retrieval.
checkpoints: Evaluate passage relevance before generation.
Check citation version and groundedness.
Propagate document deletion and access changes.

briefing.whyItMatters: Good retrieval and good generation are separate outcomes that need separate checks.
briefing.takeaway: Evaluate evidence selection and answer support independently.

lessons.title: Publish data products with an access contract
lessons.lead: Share the usable subset and keep ownership explicit.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: An authorized view can expose a selected query result without granting direct access to source tables. BigQuery sharing, also known as Analytics Hub, distributes governed listings that consumers can subscribe to.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose a view for a restricted shape of data and a listing for reusable discovery and subscription. Document freshness, location, cost responsibility and who can grant access.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A partner needs only aggregated regional sales. Expose the permitted aggregation and publish its contract; do not grant broad access to raw customer rows.

sections.title: Publish a data-access contract
sections.body: An exchange or listing gives consumers a discoverable access path; it does not explain the business meaning by itself. Record ownership, permitted audience, location, freshness, quality and cost responsibility. A consumer needs to know whether they are seeing raw observations, corrected totals or a periodically refreshed snapshot.

sections.title: Expose only the required shape
sections.body: Use an authorized view when a selected query result fits the sharing requirement. Use row or column controls when the underlying read policy needs to vary by identity or data field. Check the effective consumer grants and the authorization relationship instead of assuming a report link grants the intended data access.

sections.title: Plan change and revocation behavior
sections.body: A producer can change schemas, retire a product or revoke access. Document which changes are compatible and how consumers learn about them. Avoid teaching third-party sharing as a one-time export when the requirement is governed, reusable access to current data.

lessons.trap: Sharing a report URL does not automatically authorize the viewer to its underlying data.

exercise.prompt: A partner subscribes to a listing but misinterprets a revenue field as net revenue. What was missing from the product?
exercise.answer: The business definition and reporting contract were insufficient. Access and discovery succeeded, but the consumer also needs clear grain, metric meaning, refresh expectations and ownership. Data sharing is both a security and a semantic design problem.
checkpoints: Choose a sharing mechanism for a specific audience.
State the metric grain and freshness contract.
Explain revocation and compatible schema changes.

lessons.title: Pay for the work you actually need
lessons.lead: Tie optimization to a business requirement and a measured bottleneck.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Persistent clusters may fit steady workloads; job-based compute may fit intermittent processing. Query scan reduction matters for on-demand analysis, while capacity-based execution requires attention to slots and utilization.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Reuse supported aggregates, stop idle compute, and compare storage, processing and network effects. A cheaper worker can cost more overall if it repeatedly fails or extends the job.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A weekly Spark job runs for thirty minutes. Keep durable input in object storage and compare an ephemeral cluster or serverless execution against a cluster left running all week.

sections.title: Measure total work and idle time
sections.body: Compare steady workloads with intermittent jobs. Keep input data durable while evaluating temporary compute. Account for storage, networking, processing, failed attempts and operating effort; a cheaper instance is not necessarily cheaper per successful business run. Use a representative completion target for every comparison.

sections.title: Distinguish price models from optimization
sections.body: On-demand analytical charges emphasize data processed; capacity models emphasize provisioned or consumed compute behavior. Reducing scanned bytes is still useful work reduction, but it does not guarantee an identical percentage reduction in a capacity bill. Review the actual model before interpreting a tuning result.

sections.title: Use feedback to protect the business objective
sections.body: Measure run duration, freshness, failures and resource utilization before and after a change. A cost optimization that violates the required completion time is not a complete solution. Keep the comparison’s input volume and business logic fixed, and identify any changed reliability or operational assumptions.

lessons.trap: Reducing machine size is not an optimization if it violates the completion deadline.

exercise.prompt: A team reduces scan volume by 90% and promises a 90% reduction in its capacity-based bill. Is that conclusion supported?
exercise.answer: Not by scan volume alone. It shows less logical read work under the measured query, but the bill depends on the capacity configuration, utilization and other charges. Compare actual usage under the billing model while checking that the output and deadline remain correct.
checkpoints: Compare cost per successful business result.
Distinguish on-demand and capacity considerations.
Keep the workload fixed during a tuning comparison.

briefing.takeaway: Compare resource lifetime with the work that actually needs it.

lessons.title: Control query cost with the correct pricing model
lessons.lead: Bytes scanned, slot capacity and result row count answer different questions.

sections.title: Choose the cost signal
sections.body: For on-demand BigQuery queries, use a dry run as an estimate and configure maximum bytes billed where appropriate. A LIMIT on a non-clustered table does not reduce the bytes read. Selecting fewer required columns and filtering partitions address the scan rather than just truncating the result.

sections.title: Separate capacity from scans
sections.body: Capacity-based workloads use slot capacity and reservations. Reduce wasted work, but also inspect concurrency, queuing and slot contention. A faster query and a smaller bill are related only through the applicable pricing and capacity contract.

sections.title: Compare an original workload
sections.body: A report scans the same historical columns for many consumers. Test a narrower projection, partition pruning and a suitable reusable result. Compare bytes, runtime, freshness and concurrent behavior before adopting the change. Keep illustrative scan models separate from a real invoice estimate.

lessons.trap: LIMIT 10 is a result-size control, not a universal query-cost ceiling.

exercise.prompt: A dashboard adds LIMIT 100 to SELECT * on a non-clustered table. What should the engineer inspect next?
exercise.answer: Inspect projected columns, partition filters and estimated bytes, then the execution evidence. Set an appropriate query guardrail for on-demand use and evaluate capacity behavior separately.
checkpoints: Identify the pricing model.
Separate result rows from scanned bytes.
Measure freshness as well as runtime.

decision.advantage: Cost controls can prevent an unexpectedly large scan before it runs.
decision.limitation: An estimate or a local scan model is not a production bill.
decision.useCase: Reduce repeated dashboard work while preserving the required freshness.

briefing.whyItMatters: On a non-clustered BigQuery table, fewer returned rows do not mean fewer bytes read.
briefing.takeaway: Separate result size, scan work and the applicable pricing model.

lessons.title: Make every retry intentional
lessons.lead: A directed acyclic graph makes task dependencies visible.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Composer uses Airflow DAGs for scheduled workflows with task dependencies. Workflows coordinates service calls without managing an Airflow environment. An idempotent task supports safer retries and partial reruns.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use separate tasks when separate failure recovery matters. Pass a stable run identifier, make writes repeatable, and define completion and failure alerts.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A daily process fetches files, decrypts them and runs SQL. Separate DAG tasks allow rerunning only the failed stage while preserving evidence of successful earlier stages.

sections.title: Make run identity explicit
sections.body: A task should know the logical input interval or batch it is processing. A retry, delayed execution or historical backfill should not silently switch to whatever the wall clock calls today. Use that logical interval to choose inputs and output keys, and record the code or configuration version used.

sections.title: Choose boundaries that support recovery
sections.body: Separate fetch, decryption, staging, transformation and validation when they need independent retries. Make each task’s effects repeatable or transactional where possible. A task should succeed only after its expected output is usable; catching every error and reporting success defeats downstream dependency logic.

sections.title: A quality check must gate the consumer
sections.body: An assertion existing in a repository does not automatically mean every downstream action waits for it. Declare and test the appropriate assertion dependencies. Run a known failing input and verify that the curated consumer is blocked, rather than checking only that the assertion produced a red status somewhere.

lessons.trap: Putting the entire process inside one operator hides the recovery boundaries.
lessons.code:
# Illustrative DAG dependencies, not a full deployable DAG.
fetch_files >> decrypt_files >> load_staging >> transform_sql >> validate

exercise.prompt: A backfill for last month queries CURRENT_DATE and appends into today’s target. What should change?
exercise.answer: Parameterize the logical interval and define a repeatable write strategy for that interval. Use stable keys or replacement boundaries and gate publication on quality checks. Test the same interval twice and confirm that the resulting business total does not double.
checkpoints: Use logical intervals for retries and backfills.
Make task effects repeatable.
Prove that failed quality checks block publication.

lessons.title: Make orchestration safe to retry
lessons.lead: A schedule coordinates tasks; deterministic inputs and controlled side effects make retries safe.

sections.title: Separate orchestration and execution
sections.body: Cloud Composer terminology appears in the exam guide; current documentation uses Managed Airflow. DAGs describe tasks and their dependencies. Let specialized services perform the large transformation while the orchestration layer starts, observes and coordinates the work.

sections.title: Pin the logical input
sections.body: Airflow recommends repeatable task effects and reading a specific data partition. A retry that reads latest data can see different inputs. Use the intended interval and stable outputs, then make publication depend on validation. Avoid passing required durable data through a worker-local file.

sections.title: Rehearse a partial failure
sections.body: Original scenario: a daily load succeeds but its notification task fails. Re-running should not append the same business rows again. Record the interval and operation identity, use an appropriate idempotent write pattern and test the failure after each durable side effect.

lessons.trap: A green DAG does not prove the produced data satisfies the business contract.

exercise.prompt: A retried task uses the current clock to choose its input folder. What changes?
exercise.answer: A later retry can read a different interval. Pin the logical input and output and verify idempotent effects, including downstream publication.
checkpoints: Pin the data interval.
Identify every durable side effect.
Block publication on quality.

decision.advantage: Explicit dependencies make recovery and ownership easier to reason about.
decision.limitation: Orchestrator success does not validate data correctness automatically.
decision.useCase: Recover a failed daily pipeline without publishing duplicate business rows.

briefing.whyItMatters: Using the current clock or blindly appending can change the input or duplicate the output.

lessons.title: Keep competing workloads from interfering
lessons.lead: Priority and capacity allocation are different controls.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: BigQuery reservations assign compute capacity to workloads. Baseline capacity and autoscaling affect resource availability and spend. Separate reservations can isolate dashboard work from heavy transformation jobs.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Measure usage before sizing capacity. Choose interactive or batch execution according to latency tolerance, and use reservation assignments for the intended projects or workloads.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Dashboards slow down during ETL. Assign them a deliberate capacity pool and place cost-sensitive ETL in another allocation rather than assuming an interactive label reserves resources.

sections.title: Separate resource isolation from job priority
sections.body: Interactive and batch priority describe execution behavior; reservation assignments allocate workload capacity. A latency-sensitive team can still compete for a shared pool if it has no deliberate resource boundary. Use measurements to choose assignments and capacity rather than assuming a priority label guarantees a dedicated allocation.

sections.title: Reason about baseline and elasticity
sections.body: Baseline capacity supplies a configured starting allocation. Autoscaling can add capacity according to the supported configuration and workload. The maximum is a capacity setting, not a complete fixed-spend guarantee across storage and other services. Inspect edition, assignment, idle sharing and usage behavior under the chosen configuration.

sections.title: Read billing controls literally
sections.body: A budget alert reports spend or triggers notification handling; it is not inherently a hard cap. Query-specific controls and resource quotas solve narrower problems. Protect business-critical execution while designing cost controls, and avoid shutting down essential processing as an unexamined side effect of a generic spending rule.

lessons.trap: A budget alert reports spend; it is not a guaranteed automatic spending cap.

exercise.prompt: Dashboards have an interactive priority label but still slow down during ETL. What design dimension has probably not been isolated?
exercise.answer: Inspect the capacity pool and reservation assignments. Job priority alone does not establish separate compute for dashboards. Use actual slot usage and contention evidence to decide whether isolation or a query-level optimization is required.
checkpoints: Distinguish capacity assignments from priority.
Explain baseline and autoscaling without a fixed-bill promise.
State what a budget alert does.

lessons.title: Diagnose the failure before scaling
lessons.lead: The exact error and execution stage matter more than a generic label.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Observe freshness, lag, failed rows, task retries and resource utilization. BigQuery execution details and job metadata help distinguish slow scans, slot pressure, shuffle problems and memory-heavy operations.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Inspect the query plan and the full error message before changing capacity. Separate API request quotas from execution memory and compute availability.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A query fails during a large sort. Check the execution graph and memory pressure; reduce the sorted intermediate data or restructure the query rather than raising an unrelated API quota.

sections.title: Observe the business and the engine
sections.body: Track data freshness, completeness and rejected-record backlog alongside CPU, memory and job status. A pipeline can be technically running while the expected data never reaches its consumer. Define an actionable threshold, an owner and a runbook for the failure condition you intend to detect.

sections.title: Use the right evidence for the question
sections.body: Audit logs answer who performed relevant operations. Job metadata and execution details help explain query work and failure. Resource metrics describe saturation or backlog. Correlate these signals with a run identifier and logical interval instead of treating an isolated chart as proof of a root cause.

sections.title: Prefer a causal test over a generic fix
sections.body: If a stage is serial because of a hot key, adding workers may leave that stage unchanged. If a query creates a large intermediate join, increasing an unrelated API quota will not repair its grain. Form a specific hypothesis, make a controlled change and compare outputs and resource behavior under the same input.

lessons.trap: More slots do not guarantee that every Resources exceeded error disappears.

exercise.prompt: Worker CPU is moderate but event lag keeps rising and one key dominates a stage. What would you investigate?
exercise.answer: Inspect key distribution, per-stage parallelism and any serial work or downstream limit. More workers may not split work for a single key. Verify the hypothesis with stage-level evidence and a correctness-preserving redesign rather than scaling blindly.
checkpoints: Include freshness and data quality in monitoring.
Choose logs versus job metadata for a concrete question.
Test a specific bottleneck hypothesis.

lessons.title: Diagnose a query from its execution evidence
lessons.lead: A failure message is the beginning of a causal investigation.

sections.title: Separate queueing from expensive computation
sections.body: A query may wait for resources, scan excessive data, create a large join intermediate, sort too many rows or spend time handling skew. Job metadata and the execution graph help identify which stage matters. Compare the same input and query semantics when testing an improvement.

sections.title: Inspect the reason behind the error
sections.body: Resources exceeded can indicate different memory, shuffle or planning problems. API request rate quotas are a different constraint from execution memory. A capacity reservation can be appropriate for some workload issues, but is not a universal repair for every failing operator or excessively complex query plan.

sections.title: Use billing evidence correctly
sections.body: A dry run can estimate relevant processed bytes for supported queries. Actual clustered block pruning and runtime compute behavior have additional considerations. Query limits, job controls and budgets solve different problems. Record the billing model and the measured unit before translating a performance result into a cost claim.

lessons.trap: The first visible red chart is not necessarily the root cause.

exercise.prompt: A query fails in a large global sort. What evidence would distinguish a SQL redesign from buying more capacity?
exercise.answer: Inspect the error details and execution stage, including intermediate size and memory pressure. Test reducing the sort input or using an appropriate query structure under the same business result. Capacity information helps, but the failing operation still needs a specific diagnosis.
checkpoints: Separate queue time from computation.
Map an error to the right resource.
Interpret bytes and slots under the chosen billing model.

lessons.title: Diagnose freshness across a streaming pipeline
lessons.lead: Trace where data waits before adding compute or suppressing an alert.

sections.title: Distinguish the observations
sections.body: Dataflow exposes freshness, system latency, throughput and backlog metrics. System latency measures time an element spends processing or waiting, subject to source visibility. Pub/Sub oldest unacknowledged age describes waiting subscription messages. These observations are related but not interchangeable.

sections.title: Follow the bottleneck
sections.body: Original incident: input traffic is steady, destination writes start failing, and upstream backlog grows while worker CPU stays modest. Inspect write errors, permissions, quota and destination capacity. Adding workers cannot repair a denied sink. Correlate stage evidence rather than diagnosing from CPU alone.

sections.title: Define an actionable outcome
sections.body: Illustrative SLO: curated orders should be queryable within five minutes for the agreed population. Specify the timestamp, denominator, observation point and late-event policy. Couple an alert to an owner, a bounded recovery action and a check that reconciles missing records after recovery.

lessons.trap: A healthy transport graph does not prove that the business dataset is complete.

exercise.prompt: Backlog rises while sink writes fail with permission errors. Is increasing worker count a sufficient fix?
exercise.answer: No. Repair the identity or permission path, then observe whether the backlog drains and reconcile delayed or failed outputs. Verify the diagnosis from logs and metrics.
checkpoints: Name the observation point and unit.
Correlate source, stage and sink evidence.
Reconcile data after recovery.

lessons.title: Design recovery against explicit objectives
lessons.lead: State how much data may be lost and how quickly service must return.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: RPO limits tolerable data loss; RTO limits recovery time. BigQuery time travel, snapshots and cross-region replication address different failure and retention needs. A multi-region label alone is not a complete disaster recovery plan.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Match backup frequency and replication behavior to the objectives, then rehearse a restore. Check retention, permissions and the region of the recovery copy.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A daily export can leave nearly a day of changes unavailable, plus scheduling or export delays. A strict target below twenty-four hours needs an appropriate safety margin or a different replication approach.

sections.title: Specify the failure you are recovering from
sections.body: Accidental deletion, corrupted data, a zonal outage and regional unavailability are different events. A high-availability replica can preserve service during some infrastructure failures while also replicating a bad write. A backup retained in the same failed region may not satisfy regional recovery requirements.

sections.title: Measure the age of recoverable state
sections.body: RPO concerns the data state you can recover, not merely when a backup task started or finished. Include snapshot intervals, completion delays, replication lag and missed jobs in the loss model. RTO also includes detection, permissions, restoration, validation and consumer redirection. A table copy existing is not a rehearsed recovery procedure.

sections.title: Choose historical retention and disaster recovery separately
sections.body: Time travel can retrieve supported historical table states within its configured window. A retained snapshot can preserve a chosen state longer. Cross-region replication addresses a different failure domain and has its own supported capabilities. Verify locations, permissions and recovery operations against the actual incident requirement.

lessons.trap: Thirty-day backup retention and a thirty-day RPO describe different requirements.

exercise.prompt: A snapshot captured at 10:00 completes at 10:04. A failure at 10:03 leaves only the 09:30 snapshot complete. Which state is known recoverable?
exercise.answer: Under those stated assumptions, the latest completed recovery copy captures 09:30, so the potential data-loss interval at 10:03 is 33 minutes. Do not use the incomplete 10:00 copy or confuse completion delay with the age of recoverable data.
checkpoints: State the incident failure domain.
Compute data-loss age from recoverable state.
Separate historical retention, availability and regional recovery.

briefing.context: A dataset is corrupted or becomes unavailable during business hours.
briefing.whyItMatters: A backup exists only as a useful recovery option if it can meet the required data-loss and time objectives.

lessons.title: Prove the recovery plan with a runbook
lessons.lead: A protected copy is useful only when the service can actually be restored.

sections.title: Write a failure-specific sequence
sections.body: State the incident scope, detection signal, person or automation making the decision, recovery source, required permissions and target. Include restoration, validation, connection or consumer redirection and the condition for declaring success. Do not count a backup filename as a tested runbook.

sections.title: Measure loss and restoration separately
sections.body: The age of the latest recoverable data state determines the potential RPO exposure under a given failure. RTO includes the time to detect and execute recovery, validate data and resume the business path. A fast copy operation does not prove a short end-to-end restoration objective.

sections.title: Rehearse with representative constraints
sections.body: A test should demonstrate the intended failure domain without corrupting production. Validate data totals, access, key availability and downstream behavior in the recovery environment. Record which assumptions were simulated, which were observed and what remains untested.

lessons.trap: Replication can reproduce a bad application write; availability does not replace historical recovery.

exercise.prompt: The backup restores successfully but the application account cannot read it. Has RTO been met?
exercise.answer: No, if the business service has not resumed. Access and consumer validation belong in the measured recovery procedure. Review the required roles, key permissions and redirection steps before declaring restoration complete.
checkpoints: Define the incident scope.
Measure recoverable-state age.
Include consumers and permissions in recovery evidence.

glossary.meaning: The time between a request or event and its result.

questions.sourceExplanation: The symptoms described—strong performance on training data but poor performance on new data—are the definition of overfitting. Dropout is a regularization technique that prevents overfitting by randomly disabling neurons during training, forcing the network to learn more robust features and improving generalization. Threading addresses computational speed, serialization handles model persistence, and dimensionality reduction modifies input features, none of which directly solve the structural overfitting issue caused by excessive model complexity.

questions.sourceExplanation:
To handle duplicates from BigQuery streaming inserts, you must deduplicate rows based on the unique ID. 
The ROW_NUMBER() window function assigned over PARTITION BY unique ID allows you to rank duplicate rows and filter for only the first occurrence (WHERE row = 1). 
This ensures exactly one row per unique ID is returned, whereas GROUP BY aggregates data rather than removing duplicates, LAG filters out unique records, and ORDER BY with LIMIT returns a single row globally.

To enforce the principle of least privilege in BigQuery, you must actively restrict access and structure data for granular control.

questions.sourceExplanation:
BigQuery streaming inserts provide eventual consistency, meaning data may not be immediately available for querying due to internal buffering.
Option D is the correct answer in the context of this exam question because it suggests adjusting the application logic to wait for a period longer than the estimated latency (e.g., twice the average) before running queries, ensuring the data has been flushed and is visible.
This approach acknowledges the inherent delay of streaming inserts without switching to batch loads or external databases, which would violate the near real-time requirement.
questions.explanation: Waiting twice an observed average does not bound worst-case freshness or prove strong consistency. Design around documented write visibility, delivery contracts and explicit completeness checks rather than treating an average delay as a guarantee. The original key is preserved for comparison only.

Flowlogistic Case Study -

Company Overview -
Flowlogistic is a leading logistics and supply chain provider. They help businesses throughout the world manage their resources and transport them to their final destination. The company has grown rapidly, expanding their offerings to include rail, truck, aircraft, and oceanic shipping.

Company Background -
The company started as a regional trucking company, and then expanded into other logistics market. Because they have not updated their infrastructure, managing and tracking orders and shipments has become a bottleneck. To improve operations, Flowlogistic developed proprietary technology for tracking shipments in real time at the parcel level. However, they are unable to deploy it because their technology stack, based on Apache Kafka, cannot support the processing volume. In addition, Flowlogistic wants to further analyze their orders and shipments to determine how best to deploy their resources.

Solution Concept -
Flowlogistic wants to implement two concepts using the cloud:
✑ Use their proprietary technology in a real-time inventory-tracking system that indicates the location of their loads
✑ Perform analytics on all their orders and shipment logs, which contain both structured and unstructured data, to determine how best to deploy resources, which markets to expand info. They also want to use predictive analytics to learn earlier when a shipment will be delayed.

Existing Technical Environment -
Flowlogistic architecture resides in a single data center:
✑ Databases
8 physical servers in 2 clusters
- SQL Server `" user data, inventory, static data
3 physical servers
- Cassandra `" metadata, tracking messages
10 Kafka servers `" tracking message aggregation and batch insert
✑ Application servers `" customer front end, middleware for order/customs
60 virtual machines across 20 physical servers
- Tomcat `" Java services
- Nginx `" static content
- Batch servers
✑ Storage appliances
-  iSCSI for virtual machine (VM) hosts
-  Fibre Channel storage area network (FC SAN) `" SQL server storage
-  Network-attached storage (NAS) image storage, logs, backups
✑ 10 Apache Hadoop /Spark servers
- Core Data Lake
- Data analysis workloads
✑ 20 miscellaneous servers
- Jenkins, monitoring, bastion hosts,

Business Requirements -
Build a reliable and reproducible environment with scaled panty of production.

✑ Aggregate data in a centralized Data Lake for analysis
✑ Use historical data to perform predictive analytics on future shipments
✑ Accurately track every shipment worldwide using proprietary technology
✑ Improve business agility and speed of innovation through rapid provisioning of new resources
✑ Analyze and optimize architecture for performance in the cloud
✑ Migrate fully to the cloud if all other requirements are met

Technical Requirements -
✑ Handle both streaming and batch data
✑ Migrate existing Hadoop workloads
✑ Ensure architecture is scalable and elastic to meet the changing demands of the company.
✑ Use managed services whenever possible
✑ Encrypt data flight and at rest
✑ Connect a VPN between the production data center and cloud environment

SEO Statement -
We have grown so quickly that our inability to upgrade our infrastructure is really hampering further growth and efficiency. We are efficient at moving shipments around the world, but we are inefficient at moving data around.
We need to organize our information so we can more easily understand where our customers are and what they are shipping.

CTO Statement -
IT has never been a priority for us, so as our data has grown, we have not invested enough in our technology. I have a good staff to manage IT, but they are so busy managing our infrastructure that I cannot get them to do the things that really matter, such as organizing our data, building the analytics, and figuring out how to implement the CFO' s tracking technology.

CFO Statement -
Part of our competitive advantage is that we penalize ourselves for late shipments and deliveries. Knowing where out shipments are at all times has a direct correlation to our bottom line and profitability. Additionally, I don't want to commit capital to building out a server environment.
Flowlogistic wants to use Google BigQuery as their primary analysis system, but they still have Apache Hadoop and Spark workloads that they cannot move to
BigQuery. Flowlogistic does not know how to store the data that is common to both workloads. What should they do?

questions.sourceExplanation:
Google Cloud Storage (GCS) serves as the central data lake in Google Cloud Platform, providing a unified storage layer for both BigQuery and Dataproc (Hadoop/Spark).
Avro is an open-source serialization format that is natively supported by both systems, allowing them to read the same common data without duplication or complex connector configurations.

MJTelco Case Study -

Company Overview -
MJTelco is a startup that plans to build networks in rapidly growing, underserved markets around the world. The company has patents for innovative optical communications hardware. Based on these patents, they can create many reliable, high-speed backbone links with inexpensive hardware.

Company Background -
Founded by experienced telecom executives, MJTelco uses technologies originally developed to overcome communications challenges in space. Fundamental to their operation, they need to create a distributed data infrastructure that drives real-time analysis and incorporates machine learning to continuously optimize their topologies. Because their hardware is inexpensive, they plan to overdeploy the network allowing them to account for the impact of dynamic regional politics on location availability and cost.
Their management and operations teams are situated all around the globe creating many-to-many relationship between data consumers and provides in their system. After careful consideration, they decided public cloud is the perfect environment to support their needs.

Solution Concept -
MJTelco is running a successful proof-of-concept (PoC) project in its labs. They have two primary needs:
✑ Scale and harden their PoC to support significantly more data flows generated when they ramp to more than 50,000 installations.
✑ Refine their machine-learning cycles to verify and improve the dynamic models they use to control topology definition.
MJTelco will also use three separate operating environments `" development/test, staging, and production `" to meet the needs of running experiments, deploying new features, and serving production customers.

Business Requirements -
✑ Scale up their production environment with minimal cost, instantiating resources when and where needed in an unpredictable, distributed telecom user community.
✑ Ensure security of their proprietary data to protect their leading-edge machine learning and analysis.
✑ Provide reliable and timely access to data for analysis from distributed research workers
✑ Maintain isolated environments that support rapid iteration of their machine-learning models without affecting their customers.

Technical Requirements -

questions.sourceExplanation:
Bigtable rowkeys must be designed to avoid hotspotting by ensuring writes are distributed across multiple nodes. Using 'date' or 'timestamp' as the leading component of a rowkey creates severe write hotspots because all devices update on the same time interval, overwhelming specific nodes.

Option A is the best available choice because placing 'date' first groups data chronologically, which supports the most common query pattern (retrieving all data for a given device on a given day) efficiently via range scans. While an ideal schema might reverse this or use salting to balance writes, Option A effectively satisfies the read-heavy analytical requirement without creating the extreme concentration of writes that pure timestamp keys cause.

Option C is correct because using `gsutil` with parallel uploads (`-m`) efficiently handles a high volume of small files by leveraging multi-threading, overcoming the per-file overhead inherent in the current SFTP design.

choices.html: Most rows in the [myproject:mydataset.mytable] table have the same value in the country column, causing data skew

questions.sourceExplanation:
The query plan image indicates a significant imbalance in the processing stages, which is a hallmark of data skew.
When most rows share the same key value (e.g., 'country'), BigQuery cannot evenly distribute the work across workers during the shuffle phase, causing some nodes to process disproportionately more data than others.
This uneven distribution forces the query to wait for the slowest worker to finish, resulting in the observed delay regardless of concurrency or partition count.

Engineers have decided to use windowing and transformation in Google Cloud Dataflow for this purpose. However, when testing this feature, they find that the Cloud Dataflow job fails for the all streaming insert. What is the most likely cause of this problem?
questions.html: Your company is currently setting up data pipelines for their campaign. For all the Google Cloud Pub/Sub streaming data, one of the important business requirements is to be able to periodically identify the inputs and their timings during their campaign. Engineers have decided to use windowing and transformation in Google Cloud Dataflow for this purpose. However, when testing this feature, they find that the Cloud Dataflow job fails for the all streaming insert. What is the most likely cause of this problem?

choices.text: They have not assigned the timestamp, which causes the job to fail
choices.html: They have not assigned the timestamp, which causes the job to fail

choices.text: They have not set the triggers to accommodate the data coming in late, which causes the job to fail
choices.html: They have not set the triggers to accommodate the data coming in late, which causes the job to fail

choices.text: They have not applied a global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created
choices.html: They have not applied a global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created

choices.text: They have not applied a non-global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created
choices.html: They have not applied a non-global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created

questions.sourceExplanation: In Apache Beam and Google Cloud Dataflow, unbounded (streaming) PCollections default to a GlobalWindow. If you apply grouping transforms like GroupByKey or Combine to a streaming PCollection without setting a non-global windowing function or a custom trigger, the pipeline will throw an error upon construction because it waits indefinitely for all data to arrive. Therefore, the failure is caused by the absence of a non-global windowing function.

Modifying existing transform jobs (Option A) would require changes to multiple computational steps, increasing complexity and maintenance overhead without isolating the correction logic.

questions.sourceExplanation:
The issue stems from using date-sharded tables (one table per day), which exceeds BigQuery's 1,000-table limit when querying over long ranges.
Converting these multiple sharded tables into a single partitioned table consolidates the data into one entity, thereby eliminating the table count restriction while maintaining efficient query performance through partition pruning.

Watermarks specifically handle late or out-of-order data by defining allowed lateness, ensuring the pipeline processes data within a predictable time window while accommodating delays.

questions.text: You have some data, which is shown in the graphic below. The two dimensions are X and Y, and the shade of each dot represents what class it is. You want to classify this data accurately using a linear algorithm. To do this you need to add a synthetic feature. What should the value of that feature be?
questions.html: You have some data, which is shown in the graphic below. The two dimensions are X and Y, and the shade of each dot represents what class it is. You want to classify this data accurately using a linear algorithm. To do this you need to add a synthetic feature. What should the value of that feature be?

choices.text: X2+Y2
choices.html: X2+Y2

choices.text: X2
choices.html: X2

choices.text: Y2
choices.html: Y2

choices.text: cos(X)
choices.html: cos(X)

questions.sourceExplanation: The data exhibits a circular decision boundary, which is non-linear in the original X-Y space. A linear classifier requires features that are linearly separable; by adding the synthetic feature X² + Y², the data becomes separable because points inside the circle have smaller values than those outside. This transformation maps the radial distance from the origin, allowing a linear model to distinguish the classes effectively.

You also want to optimize data for range queries on non-key columns. What should you do?
questions.html:
You are designing storage for two relational tables that are part of a 10-TB database on Google Cloud. You want to support transactions that scale horizontally.
You also want to optimize data for range queries on non-key columns. What should you do?

choices.text: Use Cloud SQL for storage. Add secondary indexes to support query patterns.
choices.html: Use Cloud SQL for storage. Add secondary indexes to support query patterns.

choices.text: Use Cloud SQL for storage. Use Cloud Dataflow to transform data to support query patterns.
choices.html: Use Cloud SQL for storage. Use Cloud Dataflow to transform data to support query patterns.

choices.text: Use Cloud Spanner for storage. Add secondary indexes to support query patterns.
choices.html: Use Cloud Spanner for storage. Add secondary indexes to support query patterns.

choices.text: Use Cloud Spanner for storage. Use Cloud Dataflow to transform data to support query patterns.
choices.html: Use Cloud Spanner for storage. Use Cloud Dataflow to transform data to support query patterns.

questions.sourceExplanation: Cloud Spanner is required because it is a fully managed relational database that natively supports horizontal scaling for transactions, unlike Cloud SQL which scales vertically. To optimize performance for range queries on non-key columns, you must add secondary indexes in Spanner, as primary key lookups alone cannot efficiently serve these query patterns.

questions.text:
Your financial services company is moving to cloud technology and wants to store 50 TB of financial time-series data in the cloud. This data is updated frequently and new data will be streaming in all the time. Your company also wants to move their existing Apache Hadoop jobs to the cloud to get insights into this data.
Which product should they use to store the data?
questions.html:
Your financial services company is moving to cloud technology and wants to store 50 TB of financial time-series data in the cloud. This data is updated frequently and new data will be streaming in all the time. Your company also wants to move their existing Apache Hadoop jobs to the cloud to get insights into this data.
Which product should they use to store the data?

choices.text: Cloud Bigtable
choices.html: Cloud Bigtable

choices.text: Google BigQuery
choices.html: Google BigQuery

choices.text: Google Cloud Storage
choices.html: Google Cloud Storage

choices.text: Google Cloud Datastore
choices.html: Google Cloud Datastore

questions.sourceExplanation:
Cloud Bigtable is specifically optimized for low-latency reads and writes on large-scale datasets, making it ideal for financial time-series data that updates frequently.
It natively supports high-throughput streaming ingestion, which aligns with the requirement for continuous new data arrival.
Furthermore, Cloud Bigtable integrates directly with Apache Hadoop via Dataproc connectors, allowing the company to run existing Hadoop jobs against this data store.

questions.text:
An organization maintains a Google BigQuery dataset that contains tables with user-level data. They want to expose aggregates of this data to other Google
Cloud projects, while still controlling access to the user-level data. Additionally, they need to minimize their overall storage cost and ensure the analysis cost for other projects is assigned to those projects. What should they do?
questions.html:
An organization maintains a Google BigQuery dataset that contains tables with user-level data. They want to expose aggregates of this data to other Google
Cloud projects, while still controlling access to the user-level data. Additionally, they need to minimize their overall storage cost and ensure the analysis cost for other projects is assigned to those projects. What should they do?

choices.text: Create and share an authorized view that provides the aggregate results.
choices.html: Create and share an authorized view that provides the aggregate results.

choices.text: Create and share a new dataset and view that provides the aggregate results.
choices.html: Create and share a new dataset and view that provides the aggregate results.

choices.text: Create and share a new dataset and table that contains the aggregate results.
choices.html: Create and share a new dataset and table that contains the aggregate results.

choices.text: Create dataViewer Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles on the dataset to enable sharing.
choices.html: Create dataViewer Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles on the dataset to enable sharing.

questions.sourceExplanation: Authorized views allow sharing query results from underlying tables without granting direct access to the source data, satisfying the security requirement. Since views are virtual and do not consume storage space, this minimizes storage costs compared to creating materialized tables. Furthermore, BigQuery billing charges queries to the project where the user is authenticated or where the job runs, ensuring analysis costs are assigned to the consumer projects.

questions.text: Government regulations in your industry mandate that you have to maintain an auditable record of access to certain types of data. Assuming that all expiring logs will be archived correctly, where should you store data that is subject to that mandate?
questions.html: Government regulations in your industry mandate that you have to maintain an auditable record of access to certain types of data. Assuming that all expiring logs will be archived correctly, where should you store data that is subject to that mandate?

choices.text: Encrypted on Cloud Storage with user-supplied encryption keys. A separate decryption key will be given to each authorized user.
choices.html: Encrypted on Cloud Storage with user-supplied encryption keys. A separate decryption key will be given to each authorized user.

choices.text: In a BigQuery dataset that is viewable only by authorized personnel, with the Data Access log used to provide the auditability.
choices.html: In a BigQuery dataset that is viewable only by authorized personnel, with the Data Access log used to provide the auditability.

choices.text: In Cloud SQL, with separate database user names to each user. The Cloud SQL Admin activity logs will be used to provide the auditability.
choices.html: In Cloud SQL, with separate database user names to each user. The Cloud SQL Admin activity logs will be used to provide the auditability.

choices.text: In a bucket on Cloud Storage that is accessible only by an AppEngine service that collects user information and logs the access before providing a link to the bucket.
choices.html: In a bucket on Cloud Storage that is accessible only by an AppEngine service that collects user information and logs the access before providing a link to the bucket.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Option B is correct because BigQuery provides native Data Access audit logs that record every read query against the dataset, satisfying the mandate to maintain an auditable record of access.

While Cloud Storage and Cloud SQL primarily provide Admin Activity logs (tracking metadata changes like IAM updates or instance creation), only BigQuery offers built-in visibility into who accessed the actual data content via queries.

questions.text: Your neural network model is taking days to train. You want to increase the training speed. What can you do?
questions.html: Your neural network model is taking days to train. You want to increase the training speed. What can you do?

choices.text: Subsample your test dataset.
choices.html: Subsample your test dataset.

choices.text: Subsample your training dataset.
choices.html: Subsample your training dataset.

choices.text: Increase the number of input features to your model.
choices.html: Increase the number of input features to your model.

choices.text: Increase the number of layers in your neural network.
choices.html: Increase the number of layers in your neural network.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Subsampling the training dataset (Option B) directly reduces the number of data points processed per epoch, thereby decreasing overall training time.
In contrast, increasing input features (Option C) or network layers (Option D) increases model complexity and computational load, which slows down training.
Subsampling the test dataset (Option A) does not affect training duration.

choices.text: PigLatin using Pig

choices.text: HiveQL using Hive
choices.html: HiveQL using Hive

choices.text: Java using MapReduce
choices.html: Java using MapReduce

choices.text: Python using MapReduce
choices.html: Python using MapReduce

questions.sourceExplanation: Apache Pig is specifically designed for writing ETL pipelines on Hadoop and natively supports checkpointing (storing intermediate results to disk) and splitting/merging data flows. While MapReduce (Java/Python) offers low-level control, Pig provides higher-level abstractions optimized for the declarative definition of complex data transformation workflows described in the scenario.

Storage from your data center through parallel uploads to a data transfer server running on GCP. Management informs you that the daily transfers take too long and have asked you to fix the problem. You want to maximize transfer speeds. Which action should you take?
questions.html:
Your company maintains a hybrid deployment with GCP, where analytics are performed on your anonymized customer data. The data are imported to Cloud
Storage from your data center through parallel uploads to a data transfer server running on GCP. Management informs you that the daily transfers take too long and have asked you to fix the problem. You want to maximize transfer speeds. Which action should you take?

choices.text: Increase the CPU size on your server.
choices.html: Increase the CPU size on your server.

choices.text: Increase the size of the Google Persistent Disk on your server.
choices.html: Increase the size of the Google Persistent Disk on your server.

choices.text: Increase your network bandwidth from your datacenter to GCP.
choices.html: Increase your network bandwidth from your datacenter to GCP.

choices.text: Increase your network bandwidth from Compute Engine to Cloud Storage.
choices.html: Increase your network bandwidth from Compute Engine to Cloud Storage.

questions.sourceExplanation: The bottleneck lies in the data transfer from the on-premises data center to GCP, not within GCP itself. Since the transfers are occurring over the network link between these two locations, increasing the bandwidth of that specific connection directly addresses the speed limitation. Internal GCP resources like CPU, disk size, or internal network links between Compute Engine and Cloud Storage do not impact the rate at which data enters GCP from the external source.
