questions.text:
MJTelco Case Study -

Company Overview -
MJTelco is a startup that plans to build networks in rapidly growing, underserved markets around the world. The company has patents for innovative optical communications hardware. Based on these patents, they can create many reliable, high-speed backbone links with inexpensive hardware.

Company Background -
Founded by experienced telecom executives, MJTelco uses technologies originally developed to overcome communications challenges in space. Fundamental to their operation, they need to create a distributed data infrastructure that drives real-time analysis and incorporates machine learning to continuously optimize their topologies. Because their hardware is inexpensive, they plan to overdeploy the network allowing them to account for the impact of dynamic regional politics on location availability and cost.
Their management and operations teams are situated all around the globe creating many-to-many relationship between data consumers and provides in their system. After careful consideration, they decided public cloud is the perfect environment to support their needs.

Solution Concept -
MJTelco is running a successful proof-of-concept (PoC) project in its labs. They have two primary needs:
✑ Scale and harden their PoC to support significantly more data flows generated when they ramp to more than 50,000 installations.
✑ Refine their machine-learning cycles to verify and improve the dynamic models they use to control topology definition.
MJTelco will also use three separate operating environments `" development/test, staging, and production `" to meet the needs of running experiments, deploying new features, and serving production customers.

Business Requirements -
✑ Scale up their production environment with minimal cost, instantiating resources when and where needed in an unpredictable, distributed telecom user community.
✑ Ensure security of their proprietary data to protect their leading-edge machine learning and analysis.
✑ Provide reliable and timely access to data for analysis from distributed research workers
✑ Maintain isolated environments that support rapid iteration of their machine-learning models without affecting their customers.

Technical Requirements -
Ensure secure and efficient transport and storage of telemetry data
Rapidly scale instances to support between 10,000 and 100,000 data providers with multiple flows each.
Allow analysis and presentation against data tables tracking up to 2 years of data storing approximately 100m records/day
Support rapid iteration of monitoring infrastructure focused on awareness of data pipeline problems both in telemetry flows and in production learning cycles.

CEO Statement -
Our business model relies on our patents, analytics and dynamic machine learning. Our inexpensive hardware is organized to be highly reliable, which gives us cost advantages. We need to quickly stabilize our large distributed data pipelines to meet our reliability and capacity commitments.

CTO Statement -
Our public cloud services must operate as advertised. We need resources that scale and keep our data secure. We also need environments in which our data scientists can carefully study and quickly adapt our models. Because we rely on automation to process our data, we also need our development and test environments to work as we iterate.

CFO Statement -
The project is too large for us to maintain the hardware and software required for the data and analysis. Also, we cannot afford to staff an operations team to monitor so many data feeds, so we will rely on automation and infrastructure. Google Cloud's machine learning will allow our quantitative researchers to work on our high-value problems instead of problems with our data pipelines.
MJTelco is building a custom interface to share data. They have these requirements:
1. They need to do aggregations over their petabyte-scale datasets.
2. They need to scan specific time range rows with a very fast response time (milliseconds).
Which combination of Google Cloud Platform products should you recommend?

choices.text: Cloud Datastore and Cloud Bigtable
choices.html: Cloud Datastore and Cloud Bigtable

choices.text: Cloud Bigtable and Cloud SQL
choices.html: Cloud Bigtable and Cloud SQL

choices.text: BigQuery and Cloud Bigtable
choices.html: BigQuery and Cloud Bigtable

choices.text: BigQuery and Cloud Storage
choices.html: BigQuery and Cloud Storage

questions.sourceExplanation:
BigQuery is the correct choice for performing aggregations over petabyte-scale datasets due to its fully managed, serverless data warehousing capabilities.
Cloud Bigtable provides the low-latency, millisecond-level response times required for scanning specific time-range rows in a distributed environment.
The other options fail because Cloud Datastore and Cloud SQL lack the scale for petabyte analytics, while Cloud Storage is not optimized for fast row-scanning queries.

✑ Scale and harden their PoC to support significantly more data flows generated when they ramp to more than 50,000 installations.
✑ Refine their machine-learning cycles to verify and improve the dynamic models they use to control topology definition.
MJTelco will also use three separate operating environments `" development/test, staging, and production `" to meet the needs of running experiments, deploying new features, and serving production customers.

Business Requirements -
✑ Scale up their production environment with minimal cost, instantiating resources when and where needed in an unpredictable, distributed telecom user community.
✑ Ensure security of their proprietary data to protect their leading-edge machine learning and analysis.
✑ Provide reliable and timely access to data for analysis from distributed research workers
✑ Maintain isolated environments that support rapid iteration of their machine-learning models without affecting their customers.

Technical Requirements -
Ensure secure and efficient transport and storage of telemetry data
Rapidly scale instances to support between 10,000 and 100,000 data providers with multiple flows each.
Allow analysis and presentation against data tables tracking up to 2 years of data storing approximately 100m records/day
Support rapid iteration of monitoring infrastructure focused on awareness of data pipeline problems both in telemetry flows and in production learning cycles.

CEO Statement -
Our business model relies on our patents, analytics and dynamic machine learning. Our inexpensive hardware is organized to be highly reliable, which gives us cost advantages. We need to quickly stabilize our large distributed data pipelines to meet our reliability and capacity commitments.

CTO Statement -
Our public cloud services must operate as advertised. We need resources that scale and keep our data secure. We also need environments in which our data scientists can carefully study and quickly adapt our models. Because we rely on automation to process our data, we also need our development and test environments to work as we iterate.

CFO Statement -
The project is too large for us to maintain the hardware and software required for the data and analysis. Also, we cannot afford to staff an operations team to monitor so many data feeds, so we will rely on automation and infrastructure. Google Cloud's machine learning will allow our quantitative researchers to work on our high-value problems instead of problems with our data pipelines.
Given the record streams MJTelco is interested in ingesting per day, they are concerned about the cost of Google BigQuery increasing. MJTelco asks you to provide a design solution. They require a single large data table called tracking_table. Additionally, they want to minimize the cost of daily queries while performing fine-grained analysis of each day's events. They also want to use streaming ingestion. What should you do?

choices.text: Create a partitioned table called tracking_table and include a TIMESTAMP column.

choices.text: Create sharded tables for each day following the pattern tracking_table_YYYYMMDD.
choices.html: Create sharded tables for each day following the pattern tracking_table_YYYYMMDD.

choices.text: Create a table called tracking_table with a TIMESTAMP column to represent the day.
choices.html: Create a table called tracking_table with a TIMESTAMP column to represent the day.

questions.sourceExplanation: To minimize query costs while enabling fine-grained daily analysis in BigQuery, you must use table partitioning. Partitioning by a TIMESTAMP column allows the system to prune data and scan only the relevant daily partitions during queries, significantly reducing bytes processed compared to scanning an entire table or using manual sharding.

Company Overview -
Flowlogistic is a leading logistics and supply chain provider. They help businesses throughout the world manage their resources and transport them to their final destination. The company has grown rapidly, expanding their offerings to include rail, truck, aircraft, and oceanic shipping.

Company Background -
The company started as a regional trucking company, and then expanded into other logistics market. Because they have not updated their infrastructure, managing and tracking orders and shipments has become a bottleneck. To improve operations, Flowlogistic developed proprietary technology for tracking shipments in real time at the parcel level. However, they are unable to deploy it because their technology stack, based on Apache Kafka, cannot support the processing volume. In addition, Flowlogistic wants to further analyze their orders and shipments to determine how best to deploy their resources.

Solution Concept -
Flowlogistic wants to implement two concepts using the cloud:
✑ Use their proprietary technology in a real-time inventory-tracking system that indicates the location of their loads
✑ Perform analytics on all their orders and shipment logs, which contain both structured and unstructured data, to determine how best to deploy resources, which markets to expand info. They also want to use predictive analytics to learn earlier when a shipment will be delayed.

Existing Technical Environment -
Flowlogistic architecture resides in a single data center:
✑ Databases
- 8 physical servers in 2 clusters
- SQL Server `" user data, inventory, static data
- 3 physical servers
- Cassandra `" metadata, tracking messages
10 Kafka servers `" tracking message aggregation and batch insert
✑ Application servers `" customer front end, middleware for order/customs
- 60 virtual machines across 20 physical servers
- Tomcat `" Java services
- Nginx `" static content
- Batch servers
✑ Storage appliances
- iSCSI for virtual machine (VM) hosts
- Fibre Channel storage area network (FC SAN) `" SQL server storage
Network-attached storage (NAS) image storage, logs, backups
✑ 10 Apache Hadoop /Spark servers
- Core Data Lake
- Data analysis workloads
✑ 20 miscellaneous servers
- Jenkins, monitoring, bastion hosts,

Business Requirements -
✑ Build a reliable and reproducible environment with scaled panty of production.
✑ Aggregate data in a centralized Data Lake for analysis
✑ Use historical data to perform predictive analytics on future shipments
✑ Accurately track every shipment worldwide using proprietary technology
✑ Improve business agility and speed of innovation through rapid provisioning of new resources
✑ Analyze and optimize architecture for performance in the cloud
✑ Migrate fully to the cloud if all other requirements are met

Technical Requirements -
✑ Handle both streaming and batch data
✑ Migrate existing Hadoop workloads
✑ Ensure architecture is scalable and elastic to meet the changing demands of the company.
✑ Use managed services whenever possible
✑ Encrypt data flight and at rest
Connect a VPN between the production data center and cloud environment

SEO Statement -
We have grown so quickly that our inability to upgrade our infrastructure is really hampering further growth and efficiency. We are efficient at moving shipments around the world, but we are inefficient at moving data around.
We need to organize our information so we can more easily understand where our customers are and what they are shipping.

CTO Statement -
IT has never been a priority for us, so as our data has grown, we have not invested enough in our technology. I have a good staff to manage IT, but they are so busy managing our infrastructure that I cannot get them to do the things that really matter, such as organizing our data, building the analytics, and figuring out how to implement the CFO' s tracking technology.

CFO Statement -
Part of our competitive advantage is that we penalize ourselves for late shipments and deliveries. Knowing where out shipments are at all times has a direct correlation to our bottom line and profitability. Additionally, I don't want to commit capital to building out a server environment.
Flowlogistic's management has determined that the current Apache Kafka servers cannot handle the data volume for their real-time inventory tracking system.
You need to build a new system on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) that will feed the proprietary tracking software. The system must be able to ingest data from a variety of global sources, process and query in real-time, and store the data reliably. Which combination of GCP products should you choose?

After migrating ETL jobs to run on BigQuery, you need to verify that the output of the migrated jobs is the same as the output of the original. You've loaded a table containing the output of the original job and want to compare the contents with output from the migrated job to show that they are identical. The tables do not contain a primary key column that would enable you to join them together for comparison.
What should you do?

choices.text: Select random samples from the tables using the RAND() function and compare the samples.
choices.html: Select random samples from the tables using the RAND() function and compare the samples.

choices.text: Select random samples from the tables using the HASH() function and compare the samples.
choices.html: Select random samples from the tables using the HASH() function and compare the samples.

choices.text: Use a Dataproc cluster and the BigQuery Hadoop connector to read the data from each table and calculate a hash from non-timestamp columns of the table after sorting. Compare the hashes of each table.
choices.html: Use a Dataproc cluster and the BigQuery Hadoop connector to read the data from each table and calculate a hash from non-timestamp columns of the table after sorting. Compare the hashes of each table.

choices.text: Create stratified random samples using the OVER() function and compare equivalent samples from each table.
choices.html: Create stratified random samples using the OVER() function and compare equivalent samples from each table.

questions.sourceExplanation:
The requirement is to verify that the outputs are identical, which necessitates comparing every record rather than relying on random samples that might miss discrepancies. Since a primary key join is not possible, calculating a deterministic hash of the sorted non-timestamp columns for the entire dataset provides a reliable method to confirm total data parity.
Option C correctly implements this full-data verification strategy using Dataproc and the BigQuery connector.

What should you do?

You've migrated a Hadoop job from an on-prem cluster to dataproc and GCS. Your Spark job is a complicated analytical workload that consists of many shuffling operations and initial data are parquet files (on average 200-400 MB size each). You see some degradation in performance after the migration to Dataproc, so you'd like to optimize for it. You need to keep in mind that your organization is very cost-sensitive, so you'd like to continue using Dataproc on preemptibles (with 2 non-preemptible workers only) for this workload.
What should you do?

choices.text: Increase the size of your parquet files to ensure them to be 1 GB minimum.
choices.html: Increase the size of your parquet files to ensure them to be 1 GB minimum.

choices.text: Switch to TFRecords formats (appr. 200MB per file) instead of parquet files.
choices.html: Switch to TFRecords formats (appr. 200MB per file) instead of parquet files.

choices.text: Switch from HDDs to SSDs, copy initial data from GCS to HDFS, run the Spark job and copy results back to GCS.
choices.html: Switch from HDDs to SSDs, copy initial data from GCS to HDFS, run the Spark job and copy results back to GCS.

choices.text: Switch from HDDs to SSDs, override the preemptible VMs configuration to increase the boot disk size.
choices.html: Switch from HDDs to SSDs, override the preemptible VMs configuration to increase the boot disk size.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Option D is correct because the workload involves heavy shuffling, which is I/O intensive and benefits significantly from SSDs over HDDs for local disk operations. Additionally, preemptible VMs default to smaller boot disks that can become a bottleneck during shuffle phases, so overriding this configuration to increase disk size optimizes performance without violating the cost-sensitive constraint of using preemptibles.

Options C is incorrect because it incurs significant data transfer costs and latency by moving data in and out of HDFS. Options A and B are less effective; while file sizing matters, the existing 200-400MB range is generally acceptable for Parquet, and switching formats or slightly increasing size does not address the primary I/O bottleneck of shuffle operations on preemptible nodes.

choices.html: Add a try"¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, extract erroneous rows from logs.

choices.text: Add a try"¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, write erroneous rows to Pub/Sub PubSub directly from the DoFn.
choices.html: Add a try"¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, write erroneous rows to Pub/Sub PubSub directly from the DoFn.

choices.text: Add a try"¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, use a sideOutput to create a PCollection that can be stored to Pub/Sub later.
choices.html: Add a try"¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, use a sideOutput to create a PCollection that can be stored to Pub/Sub later.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Using a try-catch block within the DoFn allows the pipeline to handle individual element errors without failing the entire job. SideOutputs provide the correct Apache Beam mechanism to route erroneous records into a separate PCollection for downstream processing, such as writing to Pub/Sub via PubsubIO.
Writing to Pub/Sub directly from within the DoFn (Option C) is an anti-pattern that bypasses Beam's IO connectors and can cause performance bottlenecks or resource leaks.

You need to migrate a 2TB relational database to Google Cloud Platform. You do not have the resources to significantly refactor the application that uses this database and cost to operate is of primary concern.

choices.text: Cloud Spanner
choices.html: Cloud Spanner

choices.text: Cloud Bigtable
choices.html: Cloud Bigtable

choices.text: Cloud Firestore
choices.html: Cloud Firestore

choices.text: Cloud SQL
choices.html: Cloud SQL

questions.sourceExplanation:
The requirement to migrate a relational database without significant application refactoring necessitates a managed relational service compatible with standard SQL engines like MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server.
Cloud SQL supports these engines directly, allowing for a lift-and-shift migration that minimizes code changes and typically offers lower operational costs compared to globally distributed systems.
Cloud Spanner is a fully managed relational database but requires significant refactoring due to its proprietary nature and lack of features like stored procedures, while Bigtable and Firestore are NoSQL databases unsuitable for direct relational migration.

If the subscriber code does not acknowledge messages (E), Pub/Sub redelivers them, artificially inflating the pull count while data accumulates in the topic. Additionally, if error handling is insufficient (C), the function may terminate silently or fail to process data without generating standard error logs, leading to a similar accumulation effect.

You have historical data covering the last three years in BigQuery and a data pipeline that delivers new data to BigQuery daily. You have noticed that when the

questions.sourceExplanation:
BigQuery charges based on the amount of data scanned per query. Without partitioning, filters on date columns still trigger full table scans across all three years of data, leading to high costs.
By partitioning the table by a TIMESTAMP or DATE column (Option A), BigQuery can perform partition pruning, scanning only the specific partitions relevant to the 30–90 day query window. This significantly reduces scan volume and cost while maintaining standard SQL query capabilities.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Cloud Bigtable distributes data based on row keys, and using a sequential or monotonic timestamp as the beginning of the key causes write hotspots because all new data targets the same tablet.
By prefixing the row key with the stock symbol (a high-cardinality attribute), writes are distributed across multiple tablets in parallel, eliminating the bottleneck.
This design follows best practices for time-series data in Bigtable to ensure balanced load distribution.

questions.text: You need to create a new transaction table in Cloud Spanner that stores product sales data. You are deciding what to use as a primary key. From a performance perspective, which strategy should you choose?

choices.text: The current epoch time
choices.html: The current epoch time

choices.text: A concatenation of the product name and the current epoch time
choices.html: A concatenation of the product name and the current epoch time

choices.text: A random universally unique identifier number (version 4 UUID)
choices.html: A random universally unique identifier number (version 4 UUID)

choices.text: The original order identification number from the sales system, which is a monotonically increasing integer
choices.html: The original order identification number from the sales system, which is a monotonically increasing integer

questions.sourceExplanation:
Cloud Spanner partitions data based on the primary key to distribute load across nodes. Monotonically increasing keys (like epoch time or sequential integers) cause write hotspots because all new inserts target the same node's tail end.
Using a Version 4 UUID generates random values, ensuring an even distribution of writes across all nodes and maximizing throughput for transactional data.

choices.text: Consume the stream of data in Dataflow using Kafka IO. Set a sliding time window of 1 hour every 5 minutes. Compute the average when the window closes, and send an alert if the average is less than 4000 messages.
choices.html: Consume the stream of data in Dataflow using Kafka IO. Set a sliding time window of 1 hour every 5 minutes. Compute the average when the window closes, and send an alert if the average is less than 4000 messages.

choices.html: Consume the stream of data in Dataflow using Kafka IO. Set a fixed time window of 1 hour. Compute the average when the window closes, and send an alert if the average is less than 4000 messages.

choices.text: Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to Bigtable. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every hour that counts the number of rows created in Bigtable in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.
choices.html: Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to Bigtable. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every hour that counts the number of rows created in Bigtable in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.

choices.text: Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to BigQuery. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every five minutes that counts the number of rows created in BigQuery in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.
choices.html: Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to BigQuery. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every five minutes that counts the number of rows created in BigQuery in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Option A is correct because it uses Apache Beam's sliding window feature in Dataflow to continuously calculate the moving average over a 1-hour period, triggering alerts as soon as the threshold is breached.

Options C and D introduce unnecessary latency by relying on Cloud Scheduler to run batch queries every hour or five minutes, failing to meet the 'as soon as' requirement. Option B uses a fixed window, which only provides a single average calculation per hour rather than a continuous moving average.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Option A is the correct answer within the context of this question, which relies on legacy Cloud SQL terminology. In legacy High Availability configurations for Cloud SQL MySQL, a dedicated failover replica in a different zone within the same region ensures automatic promotion and data continuity during a zone failure.

Although modern implementations use regional persistent disks (often labeled simply as 'High Availability' without explicitly mentioning replicas), Option A accurately describes the mechanism of having a standby instance in another zone to survive zone failures, whereas read replicas (Option B) do not support automatic failover.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Cloud Spanner is the correct choice because it is the only fully managed relational database on GCP that supports automatic, seamless horizontal scaling of compute capacity (nodes) alongside storage.
While Cloud SQL automatically scales storage, it requires manual intervention or custom automation to scale CPU and memory resources, failing the 'automatically scale up' requirement for compute.
Spanner provides full ACID transactional consistency and standard SQL support while handling large datasets up to 6 TB without requiring schema changes or sharding logic.

Combining the computer identifier and timestamp in the row key ensures efficient access patterns for this specific workload.

choices.html: Use gcloud kms keys create to create a symmetric key. Then use gcloud kms encrypt to encrypt each archival file with the key. Use gsutil cp to upload each encrypted file to the Cloud Storage bucket. Manually destroy the key previously used for encryption, and rotate the key once.

questions.sourceExplanation:
The 'Trust No One' (TNO) model ensures that the cloud provider cannot access your data, which requires using Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK) where Google Cloud never stores the keys.
Among the CSEK options, storing the key in a different project accessible only to the security team isolates it from general operational access and prevents accidental exposure or unauthorized decryption by non-security personnel.
questions.explanation: Customer-supplied server-side encryption keys do not imply that the provider can never decrypt data during processing. If the requirement is truly that the provider never receives plaintext or keys, evaluate a client-side encryption design and its query limitations. The imported “Trust No One” claim is stronger than the stated mechanism.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Creating a snapshot before deployment captures the subscription's state at that point in time. If new code erroneously acknowledges messages (causing them to be removed from the queue), the Seek operation against the snapshot resets the consumer to the pre-deployment state, allowing the re-delivery of all messages published since the snapshot was taken.

Other options fail because Dead-lettering (D) only captures messages that fail to process or are not acknowledged, whereas snapshots specifically address message loss due to premature acknowledgement. While Timestamp Seeking (C) is a recovery method, it requires retaining acknowledged messages on the subscription/topic, which the question states is not configured.

questions.sourceExplanation:
The question specifically highlights the use of SideInputs as a potential performance bottleneck. While SideInputs are efficient for small datasets, they require the entire PCollection to be loaded into memory on each worker, which can severely degrade performance and cause timeouts if the data is large or changes frequently.

CoGroupByKey is the recommended alternative for joining datasets when the side input data does not fit efficiently in memory, as it processes the join within the pipeline's shuffle stage rather than relying on global caching. This change allows Dataflow to scale the join operation horizontally across workers, thereby expediting job completion.

questions.sourceExplanation: The correct design involves moving data from staging to production and clearing the staging table, as maintaining an append-only staging table leads to unbounded growth and performance issues. Google best practices recommend a three-hour interval for this process because the BigQuery streaming buffer retains data for up to 90 minutes (rarely longer), making 3 hours sufficient to ensure all streamed rows are available for DML operations like DELETE or MERGE without failing due to buffering locks.

questions.sourceExplanation: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise or irrelevant patterns in the training data, often due to excessive complexity relative to the amount of data. Decreasing the number of input features reduces this complexity (feature selection), helping prevent the model from fitting to noise. Simultaneously, increasing the size of the training dataset provides more examples for the model to learn general patterns rather than memorizing specific instances, thereby improving accuracy on new, unseen data.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Data freshness measures the delay between event time and processing completion, while system lag measures only the duration of active processing. 
Since data freshness is high (40s) but system lag is low (5s), individual messages process quickly, indicating a large backlog exists in the subscription rather than slow per-message execution. 
The job cannot ingest new messages as fast as they arrive, causing accumulated delay; thus, increasing throughput via optimization or scaling workers resolves the backlog.

questions.sourceExplanation:
VPC Service Controls create security perimeters that restrict data exfiltration and access to resources within a specified group of projects, regardless of IAM permissions.
By placing Project A inside a VPC Service Control perimeter, you ensure that requests originating from outside the perimeter (such as Project B or future projects) are denied access to sensitive services like Pub/Sub, even if those external principals have IAM grants.
This approach is superior to IAM conditions because it enforces boundary isolation at the organization level, preventing accidental or malicious cross-project access without managing individual identity conditions.

What should you do?

choices.html: Create a Cloud Function to monitor all resources created and automatically destroy the ones created outside the europe-west3 region.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Google Cloud Organization Policy constraints provide a native, serverless way to enforce resource creation rules across your organization. The `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` constraint specifically limits the allowed locations for resources, and setting it to `in:europe-west3-locations` strictly enforces that new resources can only be deployed in the specified region.
This approach is superior to using Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) validation or reactive Cloud Functions because it prevents non-compliant resource creation at the API level before it occurs.

questions.sourceExplanation:
BigQuery AEAD encryption functions enable per-column or per-row encryption using specific keys managed outside BigQuery.
To achieve crypto-deletion, you simply delete or revoke the key associated with a specific user, rendering their encrypted data permanently unreadable without altering the underlying table structure.

questions.sourceExplanation:
The constraint requires Dataflow workers (Compute Engine instances) to have no external IP addresses while still accessing Google services like Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
Private Google Access allows VMs with only internal IPs to reach Google APIs and services via the private interface of the VPC, fulfilling this requirement without violating the organizational policy.
VPC Service Controls restrict access based on perimeter membership but do not enable connectivity for instances lacking external IPs; firewall rules and tags alone cannot provide the necessary route to Google APIs.

questions.text: You are running a Dataflow streaming pipeline, with Streaming Engine and Horizontal Autoscaling enabled. You have set the maximum number of workers to 1000. The input of your pipeline is Pub/Sub messages with notifications from Cloud Storage. One of the pipeline transforms reads CSV files and emits an element for every CSV line. The job performance is low, the pipeline is using only 10 workers, and you notice that the autoscaler is not spinning up additional workers. What should you do to improve performance?

choices.text: Enable Vertical Autoscaling to let the pipeline use larger workers.

choices.text: Change the pipeline code, and introduce a Reshuffle step to prevent fusion.

choices.html: Update the job to increase the maximum number of workers.

choices.text: Use Dataflow Prime, and enable Right Fitting to increase the worker resources.
choices.html: Use Dataflow Prime, and enable Right Fitting to increase the worker resources.

questions.sourceExplanation: Fusion optimization in Dataflow combines multiple transforms into a single execution stage, which can limit parallelism if the fused step is not data-parallel (e.g., bounded side inputs or file processing). Introducing a Reshuffle step breaks this fusion, allowing subsequent unbounded steps to be distributed across more workers and enabling Horizontal Autoscaling to scale up.

questions.text:
You have two projects where you run BigQuery jobs:
•	One project runs production jobs that have strict completion time SLAs. These are high priority jobs that must have the required compute resources available when needed. These jobs generally never go below a 300 slot utilization, but occasionally spike up an additional 500 slots.
•	The other project is for users to run ad-hoc analytical queries. This project generally never uses more than 200 slots at a time. You want these ad-hoc queries to be billed based on how much data users scan rather than by slot capacity.

You need to ensure that both projects have the appropriate compute resources available. What should you do?

You have two projects where you run BigQuery jobs:

• The other project is for users to run ad-hoc analytical queries. This project generally never uses more than 200 slots at a time. You want these ad-hoc queries to be billed based on how much data users scan rather than by slot capacity.

What should you do?

questions.sourceExplanation:
The question specifies that local storage space on the existing Teradata system is limited. FastExport, when used with the JDBC driver, supports direct streaming of data to BigQuery via the BigQuery Data Transfer Service, thereby eliminating the need to write intermediate data files to local disk.
In contrast, TPT (Teradata Parallel Transporter) typically requires generating local files (even if optimized with tbuild) or relies on local buffer space, making it less suitable when local storage is a strict constraint. Google's documentation for Teradata migration explicitly recommends the JDBC/FastExport method when local storage constraints prevent the use of TPT or file-based exports. This approach also satisfies the requirement for minimal programming by leveraging the managed Data Transfer Service.

choices.html: Create the encryption key in the on-premises HSM. Create BigQuery resources and encrypt data while ingesting them into BigQuery.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) is the specific Google Cloud solution designed to integrate BigQuery with external key management systems, such as an on-premises HSM. 
This allows the encryption key material to remain exclusively within your on-premises hardware while BigQuery uses the associated Cloud KMS cryptographic key for encryption operations. 
Options involving Cloud KMS import or Cloud HSM would store or replicate key material within Google's infrastructure, violating the requirement that material be stored only on-premises.

questions.text: You are building a streaming Dataflow pipeline that ingests noise level data from hundreds of sensors placed near construction sites across a city. The sensors measure noise level every ten seconds, and send that data to the pipeline when levels reach above 70 dBA. You need to detect the average noise level from a sensor when data is received for a duration of more than 30 minutes, but the window ends when no data has been received for 15 minutes. What should you do?
questions.html: You are building a streaming Dataflow pipeline that ingests noise level data from hundreds of sensors placed near construction sites across a city. The sensors measure noise level every ten seconds, and send that data to the pipeline when levels reach above 70 dBA. You need to detect the average noise level from a sensor when data is received for a duration of more than 30 minutes, but the window ends when no data has been received for 15 minutes. What should you do?

choices.text: Use session windows with a 15-minute gap duration.
choices.html: Use session windows with a 15-minute gap duration.

choices.text: Use session windows with a 30-minute gap duration.
choices.html: Use session windows with a 30-minute gap duration.

choices.text: Use hopping windows with a 15-minute window, and a thirty-minute period.
choices.html: Use hopping windows with a 15-minute window, and a thirty-minute period.

choices.text: Use tumbling windows with a 15-minute window and a fifteen-minute .withAllowedLateness operator.
choices.html: Use tumbling windows with a 15-minute window and a fifteen-minute .withAllowedLateness operator.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Session windows are dynamic and ideal for grouping events based on bursts of activity followed by inactivity. By setting the gap duration to 15 minutes, the window automatically closes when no data is received for that period, satisfying the specific termination condition.
This approach also supports variable-length processing; if data continues to arrive without a 15-minute gap for over 30 minutes, the session window remains open and accumulates all elements correctly.

You noticed that some data is arriving late but is not being marked as late data, which is resulting in inaccurate aggregations downstream. You need to find a solution that allows you to capture the late data in the appropriate window. What should you do?

choices.html: Expand your hopping window so that the late data has more time to arrive within the grouping.

questions.sourceExplanation:
In Apache Beam/Dataflow, watermarks track event-time progress to determine when windows are considered complete.
By configuring the pipeline to allow late data (e.g., using AllowedLateness or accumulation modes like ACCUMULATING), elements arriving after the watermark advances can be processed and added to existing windowed aggregates.
This ensures that late-arriving records are correctly attributed to their intended hopping windows rather than being discarded or ignored.

questions.text: Your organization stores highly personal data in BigQuery and needs to comply with strict data privacy regulations. You need to ensure that sensitive data values are rendered unreadable whenever an employee leaves the organization. What should you do?
questions.html: Your organization stores highly personal data in BigQuery and needs to comply with strict data privacy regulations. You need to ensure that sensitive data values are rendered unreadable whenever an employee leaves the organization. What should you do?

choices.text: Use column-level access controls with policy tags and revoke viewer permissions when employees leave the organization.
choices.html: Use column-level access controls with policy tags and revoke viewer permissions when employees leave the organization.

choices.text: Use dynamic data masking and revoke viewer permissions when employees leave the organization.
choices.html: Use dynamic data masking and revoke viewer permissions when employees leave the organization.

choices.text: Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) and delete keys when employees leave the organization.
choices.html: Use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) and delete keys when employees leave the organization.

choices.text: Use AEAD functions and delete keys when employees leave the organization.
choices.html: Use AEAD functions and delete keys when employees leave the organization.

questions.sourceExplanation: Option D is correct because AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) functions in BigQuery allow for cell-level encryption tied to specific keys. When an employee leaves, deleting their associated key renders the encrypted data permanently unreadable, as decryption becomes mathematically impossible without the key. This differs from access controls or masking, which only hide data rather than making it cryptographically unrecoverable.
questions.explanation: Removing an employee’s read permissions and cryptographically deleting that employee’s data are different requirements. AEAD key deletion only makes the intended values unreadable when key granularity, copies and key lifecycle are designed accordingly. The prompt does not specify that key ownership model, so D is conditional rather than a general offboarding rule.

questions.text: You are using Dataflow to build a streaming data pipeline to analyze user website click activity from Pub/Sub. You need to calculate the number of clicks for each user site visit. A site visit is defined as a period of activity followed by 30 minutes of inactivity for a specific user. What should you do?

A site visit is defined as a period of activity followed by 30 minutes of inactivity for a specific user. What should you do?

choices.text: Use tumbling windows with a 30-minute window.
choices.html: Use tumbling windows with a 30-minute window.

choices.text: Use hopping windows with a 30-minute window, and a 1-minute period.

choices.text: Use hopping windows with a 30-minute window, and a 30-minute period.

choices.text: Use session windows with a 30-minute gap duration.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Session windows are specifically designed to group events by activity and separate them by periods of inactivity. 
Since a site visit is defined as activity followed by 30 minutes of inactivity, configuring session windows with a 30-minute gap duration correctly captures these boundaries. 
Tumbling and hopping windows use fixed time intervals regardless of data arrival, making them unsuitable for variable-length sessions.

workshops.title: Deduplicate without guessing the latest record
workshops.goal: Keep one deterministic latest observation per stable business key.

steps.text: State that the target grain is one row per ID.
Order by event time, then sequence for a deterministic tie.
Predict the final sum before running the local fixture.
Check the retained versions and explain why the repeated key is not a new entity.

prediction.prompt: What is the sum after selecting the latest observation per ID?

workshops.explanation: The selected rows are a/sequence 2 with amount 15 and b/sequence 4 with amount 30. A tie on time is resolved by the stated sequence rule. The result is 45, while summing every input observation gives 80.
workshops.code:
WITH events AS (
 SELECT 'a' AS id, 1 AS event_minute, 1 AS sequence, 10 AS amount
 UNION ALL SELECT 'a', 3, 2, 15
 UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 2, 3, 25
 UNION ALL SELECT 'b', 2, 4, 30
)
SELECT * FROM events
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
 PARTITION BY id ORDER BY event_minute DESC, sequence DESC
) = 1
ORDER BY id;
workshops.cloudNote: The local fixture runs only in this browser and creates no Google Cloud resources. Any optional execution of sample SQL in your own BigQuery environment follows that environment’s normal permissions, quotas and pricing.

workshops.title: Find the revenue multiplication
workshops.goal: Explain exactly how a one-to-many join changes an order-level sum.

steps.text: Write the meaning of an order row and an item row.
Enumerate the joined rows before calculating revenue.
Compare the joined sum with the true order-grain sum.
Explain why SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a general fix if two orders have the same amount.

prediction.prompt: What does the naive sum of order totals after this join return?

workshops.explanation: The joined amounts are 100, 100 and 80, giving 280. The source orders total 180. Fix the model or pre-aggregate to the intended grain; DISTINCT on a measure can incorrectly merge equal amounts from different orders.

workshops.title: Reject invalid rows with an explicit contract
workshops.goal: Test completeness, uniqueness and values as different quality properties.

steps.text: Require a non-null unique ID, a non-negative non-null amount and an email containing @.
Mark every row violating uniqueness, including both copies of a duplicate ID.
Keep the rule and original row reference with each error.
Check the good and invalid outputs before describing a replay path.

prediction.prompt: How many rows violate at least one stated rule?

workshops.explanation: Rows 1 and 2 violate unique ID; row 2 also violates the deliberately simple email check. Row 3 lacks an ID and has a negative amount; row 4 lacks an amount. Only row 5 satisfies this toy contract. The @ check is intentionally not a full real-world email validator.

workshops.title: Replay a versioned batch twice
workshops.goal: Show why a version-aware current-state operation is repeatable.

steps.text: Define the latest accepted version per entity as the current state.
Apply only changes with a strictly newer version, or insert a new entity.
Run the same batch again and compare row count and sum.
Explain how deletes would require an additional explicit rule.

prediction.prompt: What is the total amount after one run and after the identical replay? Enter the common total.

workshops.explanation: The target holds a/version 3/amount 30, b/version 1/amount 5 and c/version 1/amount 7: three rows totaling 42. Replaying the same changes does not increase the total. This fixture assumes comparable source versions and does not implement deletes.
workshops.code:
FOR each source entity in a defined source order:
  INSERT if no target entity exists
  UPDATE only if source.version > target.version
KEEP stable entity IDs and validate final totals
-- A real MERGE needs appropriate source cardinality and delete semantics.

workshops.title: Recover an event-time total
workshops.goal: Compare the same delayed events under two explicit lateness policies.

steps.text: Open Interactive labs and process all six events with 0 minutes allowed lateness.
Repeat with 3 minutes allowed lateness, keeping the event sequence fixed.
Identify event D and the watermark before it arrives.
Explain why this fixture’s watermark rule is an illustrative model rather than Dataflow’s implementation.

prediction.prompt: What is the accepted total after all events with 3 minutes allowed lateness?

workshops.explanation: Under the documented local model, event D is accepted with the three-minute policy. All six values total 140; with zero minutes the expired early window drops D and the total is 100. The original event time, not arrival time, selects its window.

workshops.title: Compare logical reads under a fixed workload
workshops.goal: Keep data and selected columns fixed while changing query-aligned layout.

steps.text: Use the toy dataset of 30 days × 10 GB/day and ten equal-volume countries.
Query seven days and one country.
Compare unorganized, date-partitioned and ideally country-pruned layouts.
State why these logical bytes are not a real BigQuery billing quote.

prediction.prompt: Under the toy ideal-pruning assumptions, how many GB does the combined layout read?

workshops.explanation: The full logical read is 300 GB. Seven selected dates require 70 GB, and ideal pruning to one of ten equal countries gives 7 GB. Real storage blocks, plans, clustering effectiveness and the billing model can differ.

workshops.title: Map the failing permission boundary
workshops.goal: Identify the actor that actually needs each operation.

operations.operation: create the job and use the approved worker identity
read the source bucket and write the destination dataset

steps.text: List submitter, worker and analyst as distinct principals.
Assign capabilities only on their required resources.
Check inherited grants before claiming production is isolated.
State why granting Owner to the human is not the first repair for a worker read error.

prediction.prompt: Which actor directly needs source-read permission in this fixture?

workshops.explanation: The worker reads the source. The submitter’s ability to launch the job is a separate boundary, and the analyst consumes only the approved output. Real roles and network configuration must be checked for the exact services and resources.

workshops.goal: Trace task dependency effects without calling a cloud service.

steps.text: Read the explicit dependency edges.
Assume load and transform succeed but assert fails.
Identify which consumer must not run.
Describe how you would test this failure path in the real workflow configuration.

prediction.prompt: Which task must be blocked after the assertion failure?

workshops.explanation: Because publish depends on assert, it must remain blocked after the failed quality gate. If publish depended only on transform, the quality check would not establish that gate. This is a local dependency model, not a live Airflow or Dataform run.

workshops.title: Calculate the recoverable-state age
workshops.goal: Use completed recovery evidence rather than a scheduled backup label.

steps.text: Interpret minute 0 as 09:00 and minute 63 as 10:03.
Exclude snapshots not complete at the failure time.
Find the newest known recoverable capture time.
Compare data-loss age with the separate time needed to resume the application.

prediction.prompt: How old is the latest known recoverable state at failure?

workshops.explanation: The 10:00 capture is not complete by 10:03 under this fixture’s assumptions. The latest completed capture represents 09:30. Its age is 33 minutes. RTO is a different measurement covering the restoration of the actual business service.

workshops.title: Read a classifier’s business errors
workshops.goal: Calculate precision and recall from interpretable counts.

steps.text: Count positive alerts: true positives plus false positives.
Count actual positives: true positives plus false negatives.
Calculate precision and recall with different denominators.
Explain which operational cost would influence a threshold change.

prediction.prompt: What is precision as a percentage, rounded to one decimal place?

workshops.explanation: Precision is 8/(8+4) = 66.7%; recall is 8/(8+2) = 80%. Overall accuracy cannot be obtained without the negative population information. A threshold decision should consider missed-positive cost and unnecessary review work.

steps.text: Treat the supplied scores as illustrative relevance values.

architectures.title: Validate an event stream
architectures.goal: Device events become a queryable analytical dataset. Switch the validation outcome to follow the rejected path.

nodes.label: Event producers
nodes.caption: Business event ID + event timestamp
nodes.detail: The producer preserves a stable business identifier and the event timestamp. A retried publish may still need business-level deduplication.

nodes.label: Pub/Sub
nodes.caption: Decoupled event delivery
nodes.detail: Topics and subscriptions separate producer availability from consumer work. Decide retention and replay deliberately.

nodes.label: Dataflow / Beam
nodes.caption: Parse, window and transform
nodes.detail: Define event-time windows and lateness. Inspect processing mode, connector behavior and the sink contract separately.

nodes.label: Validation boundary
nodes.caption: Accepted record or explicit reject
nodes.detail: The illustrative record is checked against a schema and business rule. Invalid records retain an identifier and a reason in a restricted quarantine.

nodes.label: BigQuery curated table
nodes.caption: Accepted analytical output
nodes.detail: Only accepted records follow this path. The production write method and replay strategy must be chosen and tested.

nodes.label: Restricted quarantine
nodes.caption: Controlled exception path
nodes.detail: Retain a minimal record identifier and rejection reason for controlled diagnosis and replay.

architectures.success: The sample record passes validation and reaches the curated table. This illustrates a design, not a live Cloud deployment.
architectures.failure: The sample record fails validation. It is routed to restricted quarantine; it does not appear in the curated output. A rejected record needs an owner and a repair policy.
architectures.scope: Original illustrative architecture. No Cloud services are executed and no latency, price or availability is simulated.

architectures.title: Publish a validated batch
architectures.goal: A file batch becomes a curated warehouse partition with an explicit quality boundary.

nodes.label: Cloud Storage files
nodes.caption: Immutable input batch ID
nodes.detail: A durable batch reference pins the logical input. Keep a manifest and the agreed replay window.

nodes.label: Serverless Spark
nodes.caption: Transform a pinned batch
nodes.detail: This candidate fits an intermittent Spark workload. Test dependencies and preserve durable outputs outside temporary compute.

nodes.label: BigQuery staging
nodes.caption: Typed intermediate records
nodes.detail: Staging isolates the unvalidated result from downstream publication and supports reconciliation.

nodes.label: Dataform quality gate
nodes.caption: Assertion is a publish dependency
nodes.detail: Check uniqueness, required fields and the business reconciliation rule. The dependency must block publication on failure.

nodes.label: Curated partition
nodes.caption: Publish the agreed data interval
nodes.detail: Publish the validated interval using a safe write contract. Retrying the orchestration must not blindly append duplicate business rows.

nodes.label: Hold publication
nodes.caption: Controlled exception path
nodes.detail: Retain staging and validation evidence. Alert the owner; repair and rerun the intended interval.

architectures.success: The batch meets the illustrative quality contract and the curated partition can be published.
architectures.failure: The quality check fails. Publication is held while staging and the validation result remain available for diagnosis.
architectures.scope: Original illustrative architecture. No Cloud services are executed and no latency, price or availability is simulated.

architectures.title: Reconcile a database migration
architectures.goal: A snapshot and subsequent changes are validated before an analytical consumer switches.

nodes.label: Source database
nodes.caption: Snapshot + changes
nodes.detail: Inventory the source engine, log access and the agreed consistency boundary.

nodes.label: Datastream
nodes.caption: Supported change capture
nodes.detail: Verify the exact supported source, destination and connectivity. Do not assume all operational migration paths are interchangeable.

nodes.label: Analytical staging
nodes.caption: Versioned change records
nodes.detail: Preserve keys and ordering evidence appropriate to the source. Deletes and repeated updates need an explicit target-state contract.

nodes.label: Reconciliation gate
nodes.caption: Compare an agreed source state
nodes.detail: Counts alone are insufficient. Check keys, deleted records, relevant totals and a consistent cutover boundary.

nodes.label: Consumer cutover
nodes.caption: Switch only after validation
nodes.detail: Record the decision, acceptable lag and rollback. Distinguish analytical replication from an operational database migration.

nodes.label: Hold cutover
nodes.caption: Controlled exception path
nodes.detail: Keep existing readers on their current system while the discrepancy is investigated.

architectures.success: The illustrative reconciliation passes; a controlled consumer cutover can proceed under the migration plan.
architectures.failure: A reconciliation discrepancy prevents cutover. Investigate the missing or changed records before switching readers.
architectures.scope: Original illustrative architecture. No Cloud services are executed and no latency, price or availability is simulated.

architectures.title: Trace delegated lake access
architectures.goal: A table reader receives authorized results without a direct object-store grant.

nodes.label: Analyst identity
nodes.caption: Query request
nodes.detail: The analyst requests a table query. Discovery in a catalog does not itself authorize this request.

nodes.label: BigLake external table
nodes.caption: Table-level access boundary
nodes.detail: This pattern uses an external BigLake table, not a managed Iceberg write path. Check the exact policy support.

nodes.label: Connection identity
nodes.caption: Retrieve underlying objects
nodes.detail: The connection service account accesses the supported objects. Protect its permissions and keep them scoped.

nodes.label: Access decision
nodes.caption: Authorized data or denied request
nodes.detail: The sample policy decision represents the configured permissions. It is a teaching boundary, not an IAM simulator.

nodes.label: Authorized result
